title: Pleural compartments and procedural boundaries
summary: The pleural sacs extend into regions that are easy to overlook when reasoning only from the visible lung border. Their closed compartments and extrapleural planes explain why an injury may spare the opposite lung or enter the pleura from a neck or flank approach.

title: Shared pulmonary drainage and hilar relationships
summary: Bronchi and pulmonary arteries organize segmental supply, while pulmonary veins often drain shared boundaries and combine territories. Hilar orientation and variant systemic supply add information that a bronchial label alone cannot provide.

title: Epithelial defense, sensory pathways and small-airway injury
summary: Respiratory defense combines particle capture, ciliary movement and secretory support with distinct sensory and renewal pathways. Comparing preserved functions with lost ones also separates bronchiolar muscle tone from fixed wall remodeling.

subject: histology
title: Alveolar barrier, surfactant and repair
summary: Alveolar function requires a thin sealed interface, preserved septal area and a surface film supported by viable epithelial cells. Type II-cell repair and macrophage clearance add functions that cannot be inferred from oxygen diffusion or surfactant mechanics alone.
keyPoints: Tight junctions restrict fluid passage between epithelial cells; thickening the interposed tissue increases the distance gases must cross.
Loss of septa removes epithelial and capillary exchange surfaces; enlargement alone does not establish that destructive process.
An external surface film can improve mechanical function but does not directly replace the type II progenitor population needed to renew injured alveolar lining.
SP-B and SP-C support DPPC orientation; hydrophilic SP-A and SP-D contribute to innate immune protection. Preserving the first set does not replace the latter function.
Macrophages can ingest escaped erythrocytes, form hemosiderin and ascend via bronchioles and mucociliary clearance; in congestion they are termed heart failure cells.
examTraps: Rapid gas diffusion does not require fenestrated capillaries or an absent alveolar epithelium.

subject: embryology
title: Localizing airway-development and maturation defects
summary: Airway induction, foregut partitioning, laryngeal recanalization and distal exchange maturation are distinct processes. A preserved early structure narrows the defect but does not establish that later branching or the blood-air interface has matured.
keyPoints: The initial bud indicates successful early induction; Langman distinguishes subsequent mesodermal FGF-dependent branching interactions from initial RA/TBX4-associated bud formation.
Separate tracheal and esophageal passages indicate partitioning; the missing laryngeal recesses localize the defect to epithelial recanalization that normally creates the ventricles.
Langman includes H-type fistula without atresia. Esophageal patency excludes a blind pouch at that route but does not exclude an abnormal side communication.
Pleuropericardial folds separate the primitive pleural spaces from the pericardial cavity; pleuroperitoneal folds close the peritoneal connection.
Surfactant improves surface mechanics, but efficient exchange also requires thin type I lining and intimate epithelial-endothelial contact.
The developmental endpoint differs: pseudoglandular branching reaches terminal bronchioles, while canalicular development adds respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
examTraps: Failure of airway-gut partitioning and failure of laryngeal recanalization are different defects even if both affect the upper airway.
